title: Reading Comprehension
lines: USAT includes about five comprehension questions on a short passage of roughly 150 to 220 words. The passage may be about science, history, society or education. Questions ask for the main idea, a detail, an inference, the author's tone or attitude, and the meaning of a word in context. Everything you need is in the passage; outside knowledge can mislead you.
## Reading the passage
- Read the questions' first lines quickly so you know what to look for, but do not read the options yet.
- Read the passage once at a steady pace. After each paragraph, sum it up in a few words in your head.
- Notice the first and last sentences: the main idea is often stated there.
- Mark turning words (however, but, in contrast) and opinion words (unfortunately, wisely, surprisingly). They show the author's view.
## Question types and how to handle them
| Type | Typical wording | Strategy
| Main idea | The passage is mainly about; the best title is | choose the option that covers the whole passage, not one paragraph
| Detail | According to the passage | find the line and match it; the answer is often reworded
| Inference | It can be inferred; the author suggests | choose what must be true from the text, a small step beyond it
| Tone | The author's attitude is | look at opinion words; tests usually prefer moderate tones
| Vocabulary | The word X in line 5 most nearly means | replace the word with each option in the sentence
| Purpose | The author mentions X in order to | ask why that sentence is there: example, contrast, evidence
## A worked example

> Passage (short): For centuries, farmers in Sindh relied on the annual flood of the Indus to water their fields. The flood brought fresh silt, which kept the soil fertile. When barrages and canals were built, water could be supplied all year, and harvests grew. Yet engineers later noticed a hidden cost: with less flooding, salts built up in many fields and some land became barren. Today, planners try to balance a steady supply of water with methods that wash salts away.
> Q1. The passage is mainly about: (A) the history of Sindh (B) the benefits and drawbacks of controlled irrigation (C) how barrages are built (D) why the Indus floods
> B covers the whole passage: gains (all-year water) and costs (salt build-up). A is too broad; C and D are mentioned only in passing or not at all.
> Q2. It can be inferred that the annual flood: (A) harmed the soil (B) helped to remove salts from the soil (C) was stopped completely (D) has returned
> The passage says salts built up when there was less flooding, so the flood must have helped to wash salts away: B. "Stopped completely" goes beyond the text, which says less flooding.
> Q3. The word "barren" most nearly means: (A) dry (B) crowded (C) unable to produce crops (D) flooded
> Land that becomes barren after salts build up cannot grow crops: C. Dry is close but misses the sense of being useless for farming.
## Eliminating wrong options
- Too broad: talks about much more than the passage.
- Too narrow: true, but only about one detail.
- Extreme words: always, never, completely, only. They are usually wrong unless the passage uses them.
- True but irrelevant: a fact you know, not one the passage gives.
- Reversed: uses the passage's words but flips the relationship.
## Managing time

Give the passage about two minutes and each question under a minute. If a question is hard, answer the others first and come back. Do not reread the whole passage for each question; go to the line you need.
## Traps to avoid
! Do not answer from your own opinion or general knowledge. If the passage says something you disagree with, the passage still wins.
! An option that repeats exact words from the passage is not automatically right; check that it says the same thing.
! For tone, avoid strong labels such as furious or overjoyed unless the language is plainly extreme. Most passages are balanced, informative, concerned or mildly critical.
## Quick check
- Sum up each paragraph as you read.
- Main idea covers the whole; detail matches a line; inference must follow.
- Test vocabulary in the sentence itself.
- Cross out too broad, too narrow, extreme and irrelevant options.
